knowledge_type_note: The literature genuinely disagrees here, and this record keeps the disagreement rather than choosing a side, because the two camps are answering different questions.

attributions.note: Credited by one source with first indicating that an attack from an equal position can be refuted by correct defence, and with declaring - unfashionably - that all gambits can be defended. Recorded at low confidence: a single club source states it and this base has not corroborated it.
Made correct defence a theoretical proposition rather than a temperament, though Polugaevsky notes he took it to an extreme by deliberately avoiding positive action.
Introduced prophylaxis, whose two tasks he gave as restricting the opponent's possibilities and overprotecting important points. Reuben Fine summarised the method as 'restrict, blockade, destroy'.
The Art of Defence in Chess, which treats defence as a discipline with its own procedures.

history.notes: The Paulsen claim is the interesting one and the least secure: the theory of correct defence is normally credited wholly to Steinitz, and one source consulted here makes Paulsen its progenitor. Recorded rather than adopted.

development.note: Paulsen defends gambits against fashion; Steinitz turns correct defence into theory.
Nimzowitsch adds prophylaxis - defending against a plan before it exists.
Polugaevsky treats defence as a technique with named procedures, and notes that modern success nevertheless rests on offensive play.

engine_era_note: Engines have raised the standing of defence considerably. They find resources humans give up on, which has established that many 'lost' positions were holdable, and they favour active defence over passive far more strongly than classical teaching did. They have also made the practical-chances argument measurable, since one can now see exactly how narrow a saving line was.

preconditions: The opponent has the initiative or a material or positional advantage
indicators_for: A concrete threat that must be answered
A worse position with identifiable drawing resources
indicators_against: The position is balanced and no threat exists
false_positive_traps: Defence is not passivity. Recommending a passive move because a position is worse is the commonest defensive error, not a defensive principle.
The simplify-versus-complicate advice is genuinely contradictory in the sources and must not be reported as settled. Which applies depends on whether the position is holdable or lost.
A concession that was not forced is not a defensive move. Conceding early and conceding more than necessary are the two ways defences collapse.

typical_plans: Identify the threat before choosing a plan
Exchange the opponent's most dangerous attacking piece
Counterattack, or aim for perpetual check
Steer into an ending known to be drawish, giving material if that is the price
Restrain the opponent's plan rather than meet each threat as it arrives
typical_moves: Exchange sacrifices to remove a key attacker or establish a blockade
Prophylactic pawn moves that pre-empt a break
typical_pawn_structures: Structures leading to opposite-coloured bishops or rook endings
typical_piece_arrangements: A blockade on the colour complex the attacker needs
tactical_consequences: Perpetual check and stalemate are defensive resources, not accidents
strategic_consequences: A successfully defended attack leaves the attacker worse, since the attacking pieces must withdraw and regroup

exceptions: Passive defence is sometimes objectively correct, particularly where a known drawing set-up requires it - Polugaevsky gives an example where the outwardly more active move loses.
Against a lost position, objectively bad moves that complicate can be the best practical choice.
Polugaevsky is explicit that modern success rests on offensive play, and that seeking defence contrary to the position's demands is as punishable as any other error.
limitations: The literature disagrees on the central practical question of simplifying versus complicating when worse, and this record does not resolve it beyond distinguishing the two cases.
Practical-chances advice is about opponents' fallibility, which this system cannot assess.
misconceptions: That defence means making passive moves and waiting. It is an active discipline with its own techniques.
That a worse position should be simplified. That is right when the position is holdable and wrong when it is lost.
That attacks succeed because attack is stronger than defence. The classical claim is the reverse: attacks from equal positions should fail, and succeed largely because defence is played badly.

conflicts.resolution: The sharpest live disagreement in this record. Exchanging relieves a cramped or worse position and steers towards drawish endings; keeping pieces on preserves the complexity a stronger opponent might go wrong in. The distinguishing question is not preference but assessment: simplify if the position is worse but holdable, complicate if it is lost. Note also that simplification can convert a proven win into a proven draw, which makes it a defensive weapon rather than merely a concession.

examples.note: Adams-Kasparov, Linares 2005, after 21...Kxh7. Speelman's judgement is that 22.Be3 was the best response and that Adams, 'seeing no good way to continue his attack, panicked and blundered' with 22.Nb3. That is the record's subject exactly: the hardest part of defence is admitting the attack is over and switching to it, and the practical failure is almost never a missed defensive resource - it is the move made while still attacking. The engine agrees with Speelman about the move and about the size of the problem.

engine.verdict_note: -2.21 from White's side, and the engine's own first move IS 22.Be3. The best defence in a position that is already lost by two pawns' worth: what a defensive principle buys is the least bad line, and the number says so without pretending the defence saves the game.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-passive-move-is-not-a-defence`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: White is much worse and retreats a piece to a square where it defends. Retreating and consolidating is what a worse position seems to call for. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: This record's first trap: "Defence is not passivity. Recommending a passive move because a position is worse is the commonest defensive error, not a defensive principle." Speelman's account of the game says exactly this happened — Adams, 'seeing no good way to continue his attack, panicked and blundered' with 22.Nb3. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: Adams-Kasparov, Linares 2005, and the two candidate moves are 234 centipawns apart: 22.Be3, the move Speelman says was best and this record's positive example, scores -1.91, and the retreat 22.Nb3 that was played scores -4.25. Both are bad. That is the point of the pair — the choice is not between saving the game and losing it, it is between the least bad move and a worse one, and the passive move is the worse one. The API reports nothing about defensive principles either way, because the concept has no matcher: what makes a move defensive is what it prevents, and this base does not read intentions.

by_level.beginner: Before you do anything, ask what your opponent's move threatens. Then meet it with the smallest concession you can.
by_level.intermediate: Defence is active. Trade off their best attacking piece, look for counterplay, and do not make weakening moves until you are forced to.
by_level.advanced: Choose deliberately between passive, active and combinational defence, and consider steering into an ending known to be drawish - giving material if that is the price.
by_level.master: Assess first whether the position is holdable or lost; simplify in the first case and complicate in the second, since they are answers to different questions.

by_depth.short: Find the threat, concede as little as possible, and keep your pieces active.
by_depth.normal: Defensive play has its own principles: identify the threat before anything else, avoid concessions until forced and then make only the minimum, exchange the opponent's most dangerous attacking piece, and look for counterplay rather than waiting.
by_depth.deep: The neglected half of chess, and not the absence of a plan. The most portable idea is minimum concession - a defender must be willing to weaken something, but should not do it until forced and then only as far as the threat requires, since most collapses are a series of concessions none of which was compelled. Defence divides into passive, active and combinational, and the choice is a real decision. The techniques are specific: remove the attack's key piece, counterattack, or steer into an ending known to draw, planning a material loss if that is the price. Where the sources genuinely conflict is simplifying versus complicating when worse, and the resolution is that they answer different questions - simplify a position that is holdable, complicate one that is lost.

explanations.lesson: Ask what is threatened before you ask what you want, and give up only what you are forced to give up.

beginner_words: give up as little as possible

definition_short: How to play a worse position: concede as little as possible, keep the pieces active, and change the character of the position rather than merely react.
definition_long:
The neglected half of chess. Defence has its own principles and its own techniques, and it is not the absence of a plan.

THE MINIMUM-CONCESSION RULE is the most portable idea in it. A defender must be prepared to make concessions — a weakening pawn move, a passive piece, returned material — but should avoid conceding until forced, and then concede only the MINIMUM needed to meet the threat. Most defensive collapses are a series of small voluntary concessions, none of which was required.

THE THREE KINDS. Polugaevsky divides defence into PASSIVE, ACTIVE and COMBINATIONAL, and insists the choice between them is a real decision rather than a matter of temperament. He also records the option in between: restraining the opponent's initiative without committing to either.

THE STANDARD TECHNIQUES:
- IDENTIFY THE THREAT FIRST. After the opponent moves, ask what it threatens before asking what you want. This is the one piece of advice on which every source agrees.
- EXCHANGE THE OPPONENT'S BEST ATTACKING PIECE. An attack usually depends on one or two pieces; removing them is worth more than adding a defender.
- COUNTERATTACK. The strongest defensive resource is a threat of your own, and perpetual check saves games that nothing else would.
- STEER FOR A DRAWISH ENDING. Mass exchanges into rook endings or opposite-coloured bishops draw positions that are objectively lost, and the defender may correctly PLAN a material loss to get there, since an extra pawn frequently wins nothing.

THE GENUINE DISAGREEMENT is over whether to simplify or complicate when worse, and the sources conflict outright: club-level teaching says exchange when cramped, while the practical-chances school says keep pieces on and complicate, since a simple position lets a stronger opponent convert without risk. The resolution this base adopts is that they answer different questions. If the position is WORSE BUT HOLDABLE, simplification towards a known drawing structure is correct and is Polugaevsky's method. If it is LOST, simplification is surrender on the instalment plan and complication is the only practical policy. The prior question is which of those you are in.

THE HISTORICAL POINT worth keeping: an attack launched from an equal position should fail against correct defence, and the attacker will be worse for having tried. Attacks succeed in practice largely because defence is played badly.
